cases.title: Scalar chains map element-wise over arrays; list operators get the whole list; AtIndex variants and a byte round trip
cases.intent: When the first operator does not take a list, Transformation.invoke maps the whole chain over the elements (Transformation.kt:24-37): [1,2,3] -> [20,30,40], and a 3-element Counter read k gives [30k+10, 30k+20, 30k+30]. AtIndex takes the list itself: index 3 and its '[]' alias with -1 (counted from the end) both give 40, and index 9 gives null, which drops the channel. The chain [BytesToInt16, ToInt, Int16ToBytes, BytesToInt16] on bytes [0x12, 0x34] returns 4660 (big-endian 0x1234) - the ToInt is required, see CORE-PIPE-WEDGE-01.

assert.comment: Counter elements advance once per element: read k starts at 3k
A throwing operator wedges the whole schedule (CORE-PIPE-WEDGE-01), so every coverage case proves none threw.

cases.title: Operator chains fold left to right, keep the integer type, and a 6-operator mixed-type chain is exact and shared
cases.intent: A transformation is a list applied in order (Transformation.kt:52-56), so [Plus 10, Multiply 2] and [* 2, + 10] on the same 5 must differ (30 vs 20); a reversed or set-like application would make them equal. The 6-operator chain crosses Int -> Double -> Double -> Int -> String -> Int: 7*3=21, /2=10.5 (Divide always widens), Round gives 10.0 because kotlin.math.round is round-half-even (Round.kt:20) - half-up would give 11 - then ToInt, Str and ParseInt return the Int 10. strictTypes proves the integer type survives Plus/Multiply on an Int (operand.toInt(), Plus.kt:22, Multiply.kt:23). Two channels share the 'Deep' instance, which runs concurrently at non-TRACE level (ScheduleReader.kt:716), and must agree.

assert.comment: A throwing operator wedges the whole schedule (CORE-PIPE-WEDGE-01), so every coverage case proves none threw.

cases.title: A malformed ISO datetime string throws instead of returning null and stops its schedule's output (known defect)
cases.intent: IsoDateTimeStrToEpocMilliSeconds/Seconds wrap Instant.parse in catch (IllegalArgumentException) (IsoDateTimeStrToEpocMilliSeconds.kt:22), but Instant.parse throws DateTimeParseException, a DateTimeException - not an IllegalArgumentException. The exception escapes, becomes a TransformationException, and at non-TRACE level wedges the schedule permanently (CORE-PIPE-WEDGE-01): one bad timestamp string from a device stops every channel of that schedule, here the healthy counter 'ok'. The duration operators catch the right exception and return null (CORE-XFRM-OPS-STRING-01). A Control schedule on its own sink provides the gate.

wait.comment: Test has wedged (today: the error repeats on every read) or delivered (fixed) - in IPC its first read can come 10 s late

knownDefect.summary: catch (IllegalArgumentException) misses DateTimeParseException, so a malformed datetime throws and wedges the schedule instead of yielding null

assertCurrent.comment: The DateTimeParseException itself is not logged: TransformationImpl.kt:37 formats the InvocationTargetException, whose toString() omits the cause

cases.title: Log10 on a Double returns the natural logarithm (known defect)
cases.intent: Log10.kt:21 is a copy-paste of the same defect as Log2: `else -> kotlin.math.ln(target.toDouble())`. Log10(100.0) yields 4.605170185988092 instead of 2.0. Log10Test.kt passes for the same reason Log2Test.kt does - its non-Float fixtures are only 0.0 and 1.0, where every logarithm agrees. Pinned, not fixed: no SFC source file is changed by this suite.

knownDefect.summary: Log10 applies ln() to every non-Float input, so Log10(100.0)=4.6051… not 2.0 and Log10(1000.0)=6.9077… not 3.0

cases.title: Log2 on a Double returns the natural logarithm (known defect)
cases.intent: Log2.kt:21 reads `else -> kotlin.math.ln(target.toDouble())`, so every non-Float input gets ln() instead of log2(). Log2(8.0) yields 2.0794415416798357 rather than 3.0. There IS a unit test - Log2Test.kt - and it passes, because its only non-Float fixtures are 0.0 and 1.0, the two arguments where log2, log10 and ln all agree. This case pins the wrong-but-current behaviour so the defect is recorded and the suite stays green; if someone fixes Log2 it goes red and the report says the defect looks fixed.

knownDefect.summary: Log2 applies ln() to every non-Float input, so Log2(8.0)=2.0794… not 3.0 and Log2(64.0)=4.1588… not 6.0

cases.title: Ln(0) and Exp(1000) write bare -Infinity / Infinity tokens into the JSON payload (known defect)
cases.intent: Ln, Log2, Log10 and Exp guard only NaN (Ln.kt:24, Exp.kt:23), so ln(0) = -Infinity and exp(1000) = Infinity reach ChannelDataOutputSerializer (:31). Gson's lenient writer emits them as bare tokens, which RFC 8259 forbids: Python accepts them, strict consumers (JSON.parse, Jackson defaults, most databases) reject the whole message. Plus/Minus/Multiply/Divide already treat infinities like NaN and return null, which is the consistent behaviour.

knownDefect.summary: Only NaN is guarded, so -Infinity (ln 0) and Infinity (exp 1000) are serialized as non-JSON tokens

cases.title: A null mid-chain short-circuits and drops only that channel
cases.intent: Sqrt(-4) is NaN, which Sqrt turns into null (Sqrt.kt:22). The chain stops at the first null (Transformation.kt:54) instead of passing null to Multiply, and buildOutputValues drops null channels (ScheduleReader.kt:766), so the record carries only 'ok'. If a NaN leaked, the payload would contain NaN; if the null broke the record, 'ok' would be missing too.

assert.comment: A throwing operator wedges the whole schedule (CORE-PIPE-WEDGE-01), so every coverage case proves none threw.

cases.title: Bitwise operators And, Or, Xor, Shl, Shr and their symbol aliases on Int, Byte, Short, Long and Double
cases.intent: Operator coverage for the bit operators and their aliases (&, |, ^, <<, >>). Masks are given both as hex strings (Integer.decode) and as plain numbers (parsed as Float, then toInt). The Byte and Short branches mask and narrow the result, so 64 << 2 on a Byte is 0 and -16 >> 2 stays -4; a Long shift by 40 proves the Long branch. And/Or accept Double (converted with toLong) while Xor/Shl/Shr return null for it, which drops the channel - asserted so the asymmetry is visible.

Shr is an arithmetic shift
Xor, Shl and Shr have no floating-point branch and return null, unlike And and Or

cases.title: Byte and word decoding operators reassemble IEEE-754 values, strings and 32-bit integers
cases.intent: Operator coverage for BytesToDoubleBE/LE, BytesToFloatBE/LE, DecodeToString, Int16sToInt32 and NumbersToFloatBE/LE - the operators a Modbus or S7 user relies on to decode registers. The inputs are pi encoded with Python's struct, so the expected value is pi itself and a wrong byte order or width cannot pass. Byte and Short arrays come from List simulations (a Constant with an array Value is rejected by the simulator). In IPC mode a Short array crosses the adapter hop as Int (GrpcSourceValueAsNativeExt.kt:40), which Int16sToInt32 tolerates because it unboxes through Number - this case is the evidence. Int32ToInt16s and Int16ToBytes are covered by CORE-XFRM-LISTOF-01 because their output cannot cross the IPC target hop (CORE-XFRM-LISTOF-IPC-01).

cases.title: Trigonometric, hyperbolic, exponential and logarithmic operators match libm; NaN results drop the channel
cases.intent: Operator coverage for Sin, Cos, Tan, Asin, Acos, Atan, Sinh, Cosh, Tanh, Exp and Ln, plus the Float branches of Log2 and Log10 (their Double branches are pinned elsewhere). Each operator dispatches on Float versus everything else: a Float stays single precision, any other number is computed as Double. Expected values are Python's math results with a 1e-12 tolerance (1e-6 for Float), so a wrong function, a swapped branch or a lost Float would fail. Out-of-domain inputs (asin(2), acos(-2), ln(-1)) prove the NaN guard: the operator returns null and the channel disappears instead of a NaN reaching the payload.

cases.title: Multiply/Plus on integer channels truncate fractional operands; decimal operands are parsed as Float (known defect)
cases.intent: Register scaling is the most common transformation: an integer raw value times 0.1. Multiply and Plus convert the operand to the target's type, so an Int target uses operand.toInt() and 25 * 0.1 becomes 25 * 0 = 0 (Multiply.kt:23, Plus.kt:22). Independently every decimal operand is parsed with String.toFloat() (TransformationOperatorNumericOperand.kt:19-20), so a Double target gets 0.1f widened: 25.0 * 0.1 = 2.500000037252903. Divide is the control: it always computes in Double (Divide.kt:24), so 25 / 10 = 2.5. The docs promise 'Multiplies value by parameter value' (docs/core/transformation-operator-configuration.md:765-767).

assert.comment: A throwing operator wedges the whole schedule (CORE-PIPE-WEDGE-01), so every coverage case proves none threw.

knownDefect.summary: Integer targets use operand.toInt() (Multiply.kt:23, Plus.kt:22) and decimal operands are parsed as Float (TransformationOperatorNumericOperand.kt:20): Int 25 * 0.1 = 0, * 1.5 = 25, + 0.5 = 25; Double 25.0 * 0.1 = 2.500000037252903

cases.title: TruncAt with a negative operand turns every negative integer into 0 (known defect)
cases.intent: For integer targets and a negative operand, TruncAt short-circuits to 0 when 10^-p > target (TruncAt.kt:33). The comparison lacks abs(), so it is true for EVERY negative target: TruncAt(-1) of -1234 is 0 instead of -1230, while +1234 correctly gives 1230. The short-circuit also returns the Int literal 0 whatever the input type. The positive and small-magnitude channels are controls that pass today and must keep passing after a fix.

assert.comment: A throwing operator wedges the whole schedule (CORE-PIPE-WEDGE-01), so every coverage case proves none threw.

knownDefect.summary: if (10.0.pow(-p) > target) return 0 has no abs(), so any negative integer truncates to 0

cases.title: Result-type rules across a chain (Divide widens, Float stays Float, ToInt narrows) and string operand literals (hex, octal)
cases.intent: Divide returns Double for every non-Float input and Float for a Float input (Divide.kt:23-24), so Int 5 / 2 = 2.5 rather than integer division, and a following ToInt narrows to 2. A string operand without '.' is parsed with Integer.decode (TransformationOperatorNumericOperand.kt:22), so "0x10" is 16 and "010" is OCTAL 8 - a leading zero is a footgun worth pinning. strictTypes distinguishes 2 from 2.0.

cases.title: Every operator reinterprets an unsigned input as signed: UByte 200 -> ToInt gives -56 (known defect)
cases.intent: TransformationImpl.invoke converts any unsigned input with toSigned() before calling the operator (TransformationImpl.kt:23, 78-85): UByte 200 becomes Byte -56, UShort 40000 becomes Short -25536, UInt 3e9 becomes Int -1294967296. So ToInt(UByte 200) = -56, Plus 10 = -46, a UShort register 40000 / 10 = -2553.6 - any unsigned register above the signed range is silently corrupted by the first transformation. ToSigned is the one operator for which this is the intent (255 -> -1) and is asserted as plain behaviour. Restricted to inprocess/uberjar: the IPC adapter hop widens unsigned values to signed types before sfc-main sees them (GrpcSourceValueFromNativeExt.kt:108-111, 194-197, 279-282), so the defect cannot occur there - CORE-XFRM-UNSIGNED-IPC-01 covers that mode.

assert.comment: The untransformed reference. In-process an unsigned value is written as a JSON string (JsonHelper.kt:139-143); in IPC it arrives widened to Int and is written as a number.
A throwing operator wedges the whole schedule (CORE-PIPE-WEDGE-01), so every coverage case proves none threw.

knownDefect.summary: Unsigned inputs are reinterpreted bit-for-bit as signed before every operator: ToInt(UByte 200) = -56, UByte 200 + 10 = -46, UShort 40000 / 10 = -2553.6, ToDouble(UInt 3e9) = -1.294967296E9

cases.title: In IPC mode unsigned channels arrive widened to signed types, so arithmetic is right but ToSigned is a no-op (known defect)
cases.intent: The same configuration as CORE-XFRM-UNSIGNED-01, in IPC mode only. The adapter service converts UByte/UShort to Int and UInt to Long before encoding (GrpcSourceValueFromNativeExt.kt:108-111, 194-197, 279-282), so sfc-main never sees an unsigned type: ToInt(200) = 200, 200 + 10 = 210, 40000 / 10 = 4000.0 - the correct values, unlike in-process. The price is that ToSigned has nothing to convert and returns 255 for UByte 255, where in-process gives -1: one configuration, two results depending on deployment mode.

assert.comment: The untransformed reference. In-process an unsigned value is written as a JSON string (JsonHelper.kt:139-143); in IPC it arrives widened to Int and is written as a number.
A throwing operator wedges the whole schedule (CORE-PIPE-WEDGE-01), so every coverage case proves none threw.

knownDefect.summary: The IPC adapter hop widens unsigned values to signed types, so ToSigned(UByte 255) returns 255 in IPC mode and -1 in-process

cases.title: An unknown first operator passes validation and silently drops the channel; operator validate() never runs (negative Divide works)
cases.intent: validateOperatorTypes reports an InvalidTransformationOperator only when it is the sole operator (Transformation.kt:87-93). As the first of two it is just type-checked, and that check is skipped because the next operator, Str, takes Any (:112-125). At runtime InvalidTransformationOperator.invoke returns null, so a typo in a chain makes the channel vanish without a word. The same gap means operator-level validate() is dead code: Divide.validate requires an operand > 0 (Divide.kt:30-37) but only validateOperatorTypes is called (ControllerServiceConfiguration.kt:176-184), so Divide by -2 gives -5.0 - refuting the earlier 'negative divisor rejected' claim.

knownDefect.summary: An unknown operator is rejected only when it is the single operator of a transformation; as the first of a chain followed by an Any-input operator it passes validation and nulls the channel at runtime
